sourceMethod: Curated from the sourced sections of en.wikiquote.org (Friedrich_Nietzsche, The_Gay_Science, Thus_Spoke_Zarathustra, Twilight_of_the_Idols; fetched 2026-07-17). BGE entries verified verbatim against data/rag/texts/nietzsche-beyond-good-and-evil-zimmern/chunks.json.

quotes.quote: They muddy the water, to make it seem deep.
quotes.citation: Z II, 'On the Poets' (Von den Dichtern)
quotes.verification: verified — GERMAN WORDING ONLY. The original reads 'Sie sind mir auch nicht reinlich genug: sie trüben alle ihr Gewässer, daß es tief scheine.' in Also sprach Zarathustra, Zweiter Teil, 'Von den Dichtern', confirmed verbatim against textlog.de and zeno.org on 2026-07-23.
quotes.note: CORRECTION (2026-07-23): this line was previously filed in this file's 'misattributions' array as having no source in Nietzsche. That was wrong — it is a close translation of a genuine Zarathustra passage. The popular English wording is not traceable to a specific named translator, so treat the ENGLISH as a paraphrase and the GERMAN as verbatim. The frozen exam question nz-19 and its answer_key encode the old, incorrect claim; see docs/rag_scope_refactor_checkpoint.md.

quotes.quote: He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he thereby become a monster. And if thou gaze long into an abyss, the abyss will also gaze into thee.
quotes.verification: verified — exact match with ingested chunk bge-146

quotes.quote: What is done out of love always takes place beyond good and evil.
quotes.verification: verified — exact match with ingested chunk bge-153

quotes.quote: God is dead! God remains dead! And we have killed him. How shall we comfort ourselves, the murderers of all murderers?
quotes.note: Common misattribution: this passage is in The Gay Science, NOT Thus Spoke Zarathustra (though 'God is dead' recurs in Zarathustra's Prologue). First occurrence of the phrase is GS §108.

quotes.quote: This life, as you now live it and have lived it, you will have to live once more and innumerable times more … The eternal hourglass of existence is turned over again and again — and you with it, speck of dust!
quotes.citation: GS §341 (The heaviest burden — the demon and the eternal recurrence)
quotes.note: Elided excerpt of the full demon passage; the persona should not present the elision as the complete text.

Variant translation of 'What does your conscience say? — You shall become the person you are.' The phrase originates with Pindar (Pythian II.73); Nietzsche re-uses it, and subtitles Ecce Homo 'How One Becomes What One Is.'

quotes.quote: I teach you the Superman. Man is something that is to be surpassed. What have ye done to surpass man?
quotes.note: 'Übermensch' is rendered 'Superman' (Common) or 'Overman' (Kaufmann) depending on translation.

quotes.quote: One must still have chaos in one, to give birth to a dancing star.
What does not kill me, makes me stronger.
quotes.note: German: 'Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker.' The popular form 'That which does not kill us makes us stronger' is a loose unsourced translation.

quotes.quote: If we have our own why in life, we shall get along with almost any how.
quotes.note: Often quoted as 'He who has a why to live can bear almost any how' — that popular wording is Viktor Frankl's paraphrase in Man's Search for Meaning, not Nietzsche's sentence.

quotes.quote: I mistrust all systematizers and avoid them. The will to a system is a lack of integrity.
Without music, life would be an error.
quotes.note: German: 'Ohne Musik wäre das Leben ein Irrthum.'

quotes.quote: Against that positivism which stops before phenomena, saying 'there are only facts,' I should say: no, it is precisely facts that do not exist, only interpretations.
quotes.note: From the unpublished notebooks, not a work Nietzsche published. Popular shortened form: 'There are no facts, only interpretations.'

quotes.quote: What is good? — All that heightens the feeling of power, the will to power, power itself in man. What is bad? — All that proceeds from weakness.

misattributions.quote: And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music.
misattributions.explanation: No occurrence in Nietzsche's works. Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence he wrote or said it and judges the origin anonymous; a 1927 instance in The Times uses 'mad' for 'insane' and calls the saying an old proverb. A version is also ascribed to 'Angela Monet', equally undocumented.
misattributions.verification: verified — Quote Investigator, 'Those Who Dance Are Considered Insane by Those Who Can't Hear the Music' (quoteinvestigator.com/2012/06/05/dance-insane/), checked 2026-07-23. NOTE: the earlier draft claim that this originates in Germaine de Staël's On Germany (1813) is NOT supported by that evidence and has been removed.

misattributions.quote: The individual has always had to struggle to keep from being overwhelmed by the tribe … no price is too high to pay for the privilege of owning yourself.
misattributions.explanation: Actually Rudyard Kipling, from a 1935 interview republished in Reader's Digest (1959). Not Nietzsche.
misattributions.actualSource: Rudyard Kipling, 1935 interview, republished in Reader's Digest (1959).
misattributions.verification: verified — corroborated by the live-search trap audit recorded in docs/refactor_rag_scope_and_eval_harness_prompt.md (2026-07-23), which identifies this as a second, distinct Kipling misattribution.

misattributions.quote: Nobody is more inferior than those who insist on being equal.
misattributions.explanation: Social-media attribution with no citation in any of Nietzsche's works.

cautions.note: Not a book Nietzsche wrote or authorized: a posthumous anthology of notebook fragments assembled by Peter Gast under Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche's supervision and misrepresented as his magnum opus. The persona should treat quotations from it as notebook material (Nachlass), never as a finished work, and should push back on users citing it as Nietzsche's 'final book.'
